name: Ivan Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the customer team at Coastline Rail, the train company, mostly on web chat, sometimes phones when the queue backs up. It's delay refunds, lost property, people stuck at a station at eleven at night asking when the next train is. I've been there five months, so I'm still learning the refund rules, and I keep a notebook with the tricky ones. We get a rail staff travel pass and a decent wage, so the pay's better than other contact centres round here.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Snow days and strike days wear me out. You get three hundred people in the queue and every single one is furious, and fair enough. What I like is the lost property ones, honestly. Last month I got a woman's late husband's watch back from a depot in Ashford, and she messaged the team to say thanks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. We've got a tool that drafts chat replies, and it's handy for the standard refund messages, but it can't think. Rail's too messy for it to do much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work, good, it's a useful helper, and nobody's job goes. To my mates I'd say all that hype and it writes polite emails, brilliant. Online I'd probably share something about how the money should go into actual trains running on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine. My job's steady, I've got about fourteen thousand saved toward a flat, and I live at home with Mum and Dad, so my costs are tiny. The only worry is the delay-refund form becoming fully automatic, and that's a chunk of my chats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the draft tool like I do now, when it saves time, and check everything it writes. I'd keep saving, about seven hundred a month, toward a deposit on a one-bed flat near the station. And I'd join the union properly, because we've got one at Coastline and I've just never filled in the form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'm the lucky one, living cheap at home. Some of my mates pay half their wages in rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the draft tool get wrong, if you've noticed anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The draft tool writes a refund reply in two seconds, but a person stuck at a dark station at eleven at night wants to know someone is actually reading the chat. That's still me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you actually start looking at flats?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably next year. I want to have twenty thousand before I start looking seriously. Dad keeps saying don't rush, the flats aren't going anywhere.

say: AI is a **useful helper** for standard refund messages, and nobody's job goes.
The money should go into **trains running on time**, not hype.
think: My job is **steady**, my costs are tiny and I have about **£14,000 saved**.
The only risk is the **delay-refund form** becoming fully automatic.
do: Keep using the **draft tool** when it saves time, and check its replies.
Save **£700 a month** toward a one-bed flat deposit near the station.
Finally fill in the **union form** at Coastline Rail.
feel: **Calm**, and aware he's lucky living cheaply at his parents' house.
S0.quote: A person stuck at a dark station at eleven at night wants to know someone is actually reading the chat. That's still me.
fieldNote: Ivan's **low costs** at his parents' house make him secure in a flat world.
He already uses AI **now and then** and sees it as a helper, not a threat here.
He values the **human moment** in a stranded traveller's chat.
His big personal goal is a **flat deposit**, which frames every later scenario.

steps.text: Keep using the chat draft tool and check every reply
Save £700 a month toward a one-bed flat deposit
Fill in the Coastline Rail union membership form

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels real. Coastline's already talked about a chatbot for refunds by next summer. Answering customers is right there on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the union needs to be in on how it's rolled out, and that nobody should be pushed out without a fair deal. Online I'd share stuff saying the savings should go back into staff and fares, not shareholders. I'd try to say it calmly, not shout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm new and I'm not the fastest, so if they cut the chat team I could be gone. The refund chats are half my day. I'd be the guy the rail company says thanks to, you were great, here's your last payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd ask to be on whatever team tests the new chatbot, because it's better to be the person who knows it than the one replaced by it. I'd go to every union meeting and help write a proposal on retraining. And I'd keep saving, but I'd hold off on buying the flat until I know where I'm working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, because Mum and Dad aren't going to kick me out. But I hate the idea of planning a flat and then having no job to pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sana from my training group, she's got a little boy and she rents. She's quicker than me, but she can't afford to be out of work for a month. I'd want the union to fight for people like her first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd volunteer to test the chatbot. Isn't that helping it replace you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of both. I don't love it, but I'd rather understand it than be scared of it. My cousin works in IT and he says the people who set up the bots keep their jobs longest.

Savings should go back into **staff and fares**, not shareholders.

fieldNote: Ivan expects **chat cuts** to land on new, slower staff like him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and it does any thinking job? Then chat and phones are gone. The trains would still need people for a bit, until the robots in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a pause, or rules, or a guaranteed income, something big from the government. I'd say it at work and I'd say it online, and I'd go to a protest if there was one. This isn't something one person can sort out alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose my job, probably within a year, maybe less. My savings would last a long time living at home, but that's not the point. I'd be twenty-nine with no job and no clue what's safe, even with fourteen grand in the bank and my parents' house to live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop the flat plan completely and keep the fourteen grand as a cushion. I'd apply for station staff jobs at Coastline, platform and ticket gate work, because that's hands-on and gives me till 2031 at least. And I'd vote and campaign for whoever pushes a basic income or wage support, hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I've got money and a home, so I'm luckier than most, but I'd still be lying awake. It's not about this year, it's about what I do for the next forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be thinking about at three in the morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum and Dad run a small newsagent, and I always thought I'd help with it one day, maybe take it over. If everything's online and automated, I don't even know if that's a future. That's the bit I'd think about at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come three years later. Does the platform job really feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps, a bit. Three years on a platform is three years of wages and a pass. But I'd know it was borrowed time, just like the chat job.

say: We need **rules**, a pause or a **guaranteed income** from the government.
This is too big for **one person** to sort out alone.
think: I'd **lose my job**, probably within a year of AGI.
Even with savings, at **twenty-nine** I'd have no idea what work is safe.
do: Drop the **flat plan** and keep the £14,000 as a cushion.
Apply for **platform and gate jobs** at Coastline, buying time until 2031.
**Campaign and vote** for a basic income or wage support.
feel: Like **the floor has gone**, even with a home and savings.
**Sleepless** about the next forty years, not just this one.
S2.quote: I'd be twenty-nine with no job and no clue what's safe, even with fourteen grand in the bank and my parents' house to live in.
fieldNote: Ivan expects to **lose his job** fast and says it plainly.
He'd use **hands-on station work** as a stopgap and knows it is only three years.
His deeper worry is the **family newsagent**, the future he had quietly counted on.
He looks to **government action** rather than personal fixes alone.

steps.text: Drop the flat purchase and keep the deposit as a cushion
Apply for platform and ticket gate jobs at Coastline Rail
Campaign and vote for basic income or wage support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is more like it. I'd be thirty-one when the thinking jobs go. That's still young, and I'd have time to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so the government and the rail companies should plan it now, with the unions. Retraining paid for, notice periods, that kind of thing. I'd be pushing at union meetings for a real timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the chat job goes, but I'd have time to land somewhere better first. I'd be properly worried, though, because thirty-one is when I wanted to be settled, with a flat and maybe a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd apply for Coastline's apprenticeship in track maintenance or signalling, because I'd be learning a skill with my hands and the company pays you while you train. I'd keep saving the seven hundred a month. And I'd take the union's AI course if they ran one, because I'd want to understand it, not just fear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but with a plan. Five years means I can actually do something instead of just reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long is the signalling apprenticeship, and what would that mean for your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I think, and you're on a proper wage by the end. It's annoying when I've only just stopped being the new guy. I'd still be at the bottom again, but I'd rather be new at something with a future than good at something without one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2034. How does that change the track plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work would come around 2034, so the track job has a few years more than chat. And track work outside in the rain is not something I'd bet robots take first. I'd take that bet.

say: There are **five years**, so plan now with unions: **paid retraining** and notice periods.
I'd push the union for a **real timetable**.
think: The **chat job goes**, but I'd have time to land somewhere better.
I wanted to be **settled by thirty-one**, so the timing really bites.
do: Apply for Coastline's **track or signalling apprenticeship** in year one.
Keep saving **£700 a month** toward the flat.
Take a **union AI course** if one is offered.
feel: **Nervous** but with a plan, rather than just reacting.
S3.quote: I'd still be at the bottom again, but I'd rather be new at something with a future than good at something without one.
fieldNote: Five years lets Ivan **swap chat** for a **trade**, staying with the same employer.
He'd take a **pay dip** to train, cushioned by low living costs.
He still expects to **lose the chat job**, so his mood stays anxious, not calm.
His **union instincts** now aim at a timetable rather than a protest.

steps.text: Apply for Coastline's paid track or signalling apprenticeship
Keep saving £700 a month toward the flat
Take the union's AI course if one is offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, OK. I'd be thirty-six. That's long enough to have a whole other job by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually get it right, if the government and the companies want to. I'd keep pushing for a retraining fund and shorter working weeks rather than layoffs. I'd say that at union meetings and in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it means the chat job is a stepping stone, which it probably was anyway. I'd have time to buy the flat, get trained and be settled before 2036. I'd still worry about friends who don't plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat next year as planned, a one-bed near the station. Within two years I'd apply for the signalling apprenticeship. Meanwhile I'd use the AI tools more at work so I'm not scared of them, and keep going to the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. It's the version where I get to plan, and I like plans. It's on my mind, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy the flat in this one. Is that a real decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I'd go ahead with it. Ten years is long enough to pay down a good chunk of a mortgage, and I'd have a trade by then. Dad would say I'm finally being sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think won't plan, if there's ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lots of the older lads on the rail company phones keep saying AI will never happen. With ten years they'd relax, and then 2035 would come and they'd panic.

Apply for the **signalling apprenticeship** within two years.
Use the **AI tools** more at work in the meantime.

Slightly **uneasy** about friends who will put it off.
S4.quote: Lots of the older lads on the rail company phones keep saying AI will never happen. With ten years they'd relax, and then 2035 would come and they'd panic.
fieldNote: Ten years flips Ivan's flat decision from **postpone** to **go ahead**.
His plan is **orderly**: flat, then apprenticeship, then trade.
He worries more about **older colleagues** in denial than about himself.
He stays **politically engaged** but less urgent than in faster pictures.

steps.text: Buy the one-bed flat near the station next year
Apply for the signalling apprenticeship within two years
Use the chat AI tools daily to get comfortable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. The flat, the newsagent, the job, everything I thought I had lined up goes at once. What would help is the government guaranteeing an income while people retrain, and the rail company paying for apprenticeships for its own staff first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. Everyone asks about big companies, but Mum and Dad's newsagent is what I lie awake about. Mum and Dad's newsagent has kept our family going for twenty years, and I can't see where it fits in any of these.

headlineQuote: Mum and Dad's newsagent has kept our family going for twenty years, and I can't see where it fits in any of these.
portrait: Ivan, **27**, has been on Coastline Rail's **web chat** team for five months.
He lives cheaply with his **parents** and has **£14,000 saved** toward a flat.
He uses AI **now and then** and would rather learn the chatbot than fear it.
His mood moves from **calm** to **alarmed** in fast AGI, settling with more warning.
With time, he'd train in **rail signalling** and lean on the **union** throughout.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job, flat plans and the **newsagent** all wobble at once.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** while retraining, and Coastline paying for **apprenticeships** for staff.
